Text: Java streams are {{c1::lazily}} evaluated, meaning intermediate operations do not process elements until a {{c2::terminal}} operation is called.
Extra: This lazy pipeline structure is built by wrapping upstream Sink objects in downstream Sinks.

Text: Using `peek()` for {{c1::state mutation}} is dangerous because modern JVM optimizations can bypass pipeline traversal when the terminal operation is {{c2::count()}}.
Extra: Modern JDKs skip evaluating intermediate steps if they don't affect stream size during count calculations.

Text: `map()` performs a {{c1::one-to-one}} transformation on elements, whereas `flatMap()` performs a {{c2::one-to-many}} mapping and flattens nested streams.
Extra: flatMap merges individual streams into a single downstream stream and automatically closes them.

Text: Standard generic streams store {{c1::boxed object references}} on the heap, whereas primitive streams store {{c2::contiguous native values}} to avoid memory overhead.
Extra: Specialized primitive streams bypass the high memory layout overhead and garbage collection cycles of wrapper objects.

Text: Parallel streams distribute tasks to the global {{c1::ForkJoinPool.commonPool()}}, which can lead to starvation if tasks perform {{c2::blocking I/O}}.
Extra: Because the common ForkJoinPool is shared JVM-wide, blocking threads inside it degrades the performance of all other parallel operations.

Text: `Collectors.partitioningBy` takes a {{c1::Predicate}} and returns a map with exactly two keys: {{c2::Boolean.TRUE and Boolean.FALSE}}.
Extra: Unlike groupingBy, partitioningBy's map always contains both keys, even if the stream is empty or no elements match.

Text: Calling a terminal operation on a consumed stream throws {{c1::IllegalStateException}} because streams cannot be {{c2::reused}}.
Extra: Once a terminal operation completes, the stream's pipeline is closed permanently.

Text: Stateful intermediate operations like {{c1::sorted()}} and {{c2::distinct()}} require buffering all stream elements in memory before processing downstream.
Extra: This buffering breaks lazy processing streams and will cause infinite loops or OutOfMemory errors on infinite streams.
Code: stream.sorted().map(x -> x * 2); // Blocks here until all elements are read

Text: Short-circuiting operations like {{c1::limit()}} and {{c2::anyMatch()}} allow streams to process {{c3::infinite}} data sources without hanging.
Extra: They stop the iteration process early as soon as size limits or matching predicates are satisfied.
Code: Stream.iterate(0, i -> i + 1).limit(5); // Stops after 5 elements

Text: `Collectors.toMap` throws an exception on key collisions unless you provide a third argument called a {{c1::merge function}}.
Extra: The merge function resolves collisions by defining which value to keep or how to aggregate them.

Text: Arrays and `ArrayList` split in {{c1::O(1)}} time using a Spliterator, whereas `LinkedList` requires {{c2::O(N)}} sequential traversal to divide.
Extra: ArrayList is highly efficient for parallel streams because it splits indexes instantly. LinkedList destroys parallel gains due to traversal overhead.

Text: Primitive streams provide specialized terminal aggregate methods like {{c1::sum()}}, {{c2::average()}}, and {{c3::summaryStatistics()}} which are absent on reference streams.
Extra: This allows efficient statistics collection without object boxing wrapper overhead.
